title: Security & Compliance: RBAC, Audit Logging, Data Residency, SDLC, Incident Response, Evidence Workflows, and Risk Exceptions (v2)
author: Avery Chen
content:
Summary

This document consolidates Redwood Inference's security and compliance guidance for: RBAC and authentication, audit logging, data residency and retention, secure software development lifecycle (SDLC), incident response security procedures, compliance evidence workflows, and risk/exception handling. It is intended for engineers, platform operators, and security reviewers who implement or audit controls across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.

Goals

- Provide clear, implementable controls and ownership for access, logging, data residency, and retention.
- Define operational procedures for incident handling and evidence collection.
- Establish a consistent risk exception and audit evidence workflow that meets SOC2/ISO/other audit expectations.

Owner and audience

- Owner: Security Team (security@redwood.example.com)
- Primary audience: Eng (platform/infra/serving/runtime), Eng-SRE, Product Security, Customer Success for enterprise engagements, and Legal/Compliance as needed.

1) RBAC and Authentication

Overview

RBAC is enforced across our control plane, console, API gateway, and private deployment control channels. Authentication uses OIDC for employees and mTLS + API key/short-lived token for service-to-service and customer integrations.

Standards and policies

- Principle of least privilege: default deny, grant minimal role scoped to job or service function.
- Role taxonomy: System Admin, Platform Engineer, SRE, Model-Onboarding Engineer, Support (tiered), Auditor, Read-only Viewer, Customer-Admin (for Private).
- Approval process: All role grants require owner_team approval recorded in IAM change tickets. For sensitive roles (System Admin, Auditor access to production logs), two approvers required (manager + security).

Technical controls

- Identity provider: OIDC via corporate IdP (Okta). Employee SSO enabled with MFA enforced (TOTP + device-bound when available).
- Service auth: mTLS for internal services; short-lived signed JWTs for platform APIs; API keys for external customers with configurable scopes and rotation.

- Access token lifetimes: UI sessions: 1 hour (sliding); service tokens: up to 4 hours; API keys: rotation recommended every 90 days.

Audit signals and enforcement

- Periodic automated role reviews: monthly for high-privilege roles, quarterly for general roles.
- Access requests and approvals are logged to the access audit stream (see Audit Logging section).

Ownership

- Engineering IAM owners: Eng-Platform
- Approval & policy enforcement: Security team
- Role management UI/automation: Eng-Developer-Experience

2) Audit Logging

Goal

Maintain comprehensive, tamper-evident audit logs for authentication events, authorization decisions, configuration changes, model serving requests (metadata), and administrative actions. Logs must be queryable for investigations and retained per retention policy.

Log categories and sources

- Auth logs: login, token issuance, token revocation, SSO events.
- AuthZ logs: policy evaluations, role grants/revocations, permission denials.
- Admin/config changes: infra provisioning, IAM changes, policy rollouts, deployment/rollout actions.
- Access to customer data: data export, download, or model artifact access (credentialed).
- Runtime security events: suspicious process restarts, kernel panics, container escapes (from observability toolchain).

Logging implementation

- Centralized pipeline: Logs are forwarded to the Security Log Cluster (SLC) via structured JSON over TLS. Logs are indexed in the SIEM (Splunk/ELK depending on region) with immutable storage for tamper evidence.
- WORM evidence: For high-sensitivity events (privileged access, auditor queries, data exports) logs are additionally archived to write-once storage for 7 years per regulatory needs.

Minimum fields for each audit record (as JSON lines)

- timestamp, service, host/instance_id, principal (user/service), principal_role, action, target_resource, outcome, request_id, correlation_id, region, tenant_id (if applicable), raw_payload_hash

SLOs and monitoring

- Logging ingestion latency: 99% of events indexed within 60s.
- Tamper detection: daily integrity scans with alerting on mismatch.

Ownership

- Log pipeline: Eng-Infra
- SIEM management & alerting: Eng-SRE + Security

3) Data Residency and Retention

Policy overview

- Data residency choices exposed to customers: multi-region (default), tenant-region (customer-configurable), and on-prem for Private deployments.
- Data classification: PII (high), Customer confidential (high), Model-internal telemetry (medium), Anonymized/aggregated telemetry (low).

Retention schedules (default)

- Auth/audit logs (security events): 7 years archived (90 days hot).
- Operational logs/metrics: 1 year hot, 7 years cold archive (aggregated granularity after 90 days).
- Customer content (hosted control plane): 30 days by default; customers can opt-in to longer retention or explicit deletion on request; enterprise customers have configurable retention per contract.
- Backups/snapshots: encrypted, stored according to customer residency (match region), retained per contract (default 90 days).

Enforcement and validation

- Data tagging: All PII and customer-sensitive data must be tagged at ingestion for automated routing and retention enforcement.
- Region placement: The data router enforces tenancy and region policies; any misplacement triggers an automated remediation job and a Sev2 ticket to Eng-Infra + Security.

Controls for Private deployments

- For on-prem and VPC deployments, customers control data residency; Redwood provides guidance and repository of manifest checks used during installation.

4) Secure SDLC (Secure Development Lifecycle)

Requirements

- Threat modeling: required for any service that stores or processes PII or customer content, performed at design review.
- Static analysis: all repositories must pass SAST gates on PRs for critical services.
- Dependency management: automated dependency scanning (SCA) with weekly triage for high/critical findings.

Gates and CI/CD enforcement

- PR gating: unit tests + linters + SAST results must be green before merge to main for any service in production.
- Deployment promotion: canary -> staged -> prod with automated rollback on error budget breach or security alerts.

Secrets management

- No secrets in code. Secrets must live in the Secrets Service (KMS + Vault); access via short-lived credentials issued by the Identity Service.

Supply chain controls

- Third-party components and container images: approved base images only; attestations required for images used in Dedicated and Private deployments.

Ownership

- Secure SDLC orchestration: Eng-Platform + Security
- SCA/SAST tooling: Eng-Developer-Experience

5) Incident Response -- Security Procedures

Objectives

- Detect, contain, eradicate, recover, and learn while preserving evidence for forensics and compliance.

Incident classification and priorities

- Sev1 (P0): data breach with confirmed exfiltration of customer PII or platform secrets. Response: 24/7 incident response team activation, legal and customer success notified within SLA.
- Sev2 (P1): suspected compromise of production infrastructure or unauthorized access without confirmed exfiltration.
- Sev3 (P2): service degradation due to security control failure (e.g., logging pipeline outage).

Runbook highlights (step-by-step for Sev1)

1. Triage: Incident Commander (IC) assigned from Eng-SRE or Security within 15 minutes of detection.
2. Containment: Isolate affected instances, revoke compromised tokens/keys, freeze deploys to affected clusters.
3. Evidence preservation: Snapshot affected hosts, preserve relevant audit logs in WORM store, collect memory dumps if safe, and record chain-of-custody in the incident ticket.
4. Root cause analysis: led by Security + Eng-Serving-Runtime for model/runtime issues, with weekly update cadence.
5. Customer communication: Customer Success drafts notices; Legal approves for external communication before sending.
6. Post-incident: Postmortem and Security Review within 7 days, remediation tracked to closure.

Evidence & forensics

- Minimum evidence package: timeline, preserved logs, snapshots with hashes, list of rotated credentials, and list of affected customers/tenants.
- For sensitive incidents, forensics team engages external vendor if internal capabilities are insufficient.

6) Compliance Evidence Workflows

Purpose

Describe how evidence for audits (SOC2, ISO, customer audits) is requested, gathered, reviewed, and archived.

Request and fulfillment flow

1. Evidence request submitted via Compliance Queue (Jira project COMPL-EVID).
2. Evidence owner (system owner identified in asset inventory) is auto-notified and has 5 business days to acknowledge.
3. Evidence collection: owners produce artifacts (logs, screenshots, configs, policy docs) and attach to the ticket.
4. Security reviews artifacts for completeness, then marks request as fulfilled.

Evidence standards

- All artifacts must include: generation timestamp, owning service, owner contact, method of collection, and a hash for integrity verification.
- Live demos/console access for auditors must be recorded and logs preserved; recordings must be stored with access controls and not publicly accessible.

Archival

- Completed evidence is archived in the Evidence Repository with WORM characteristics and retained per regulatory schedules (minimum 7 years for financial/audit evidence).

7) Risk and Exceptions

Policy

- Exceptions to security controls (e.g., longer token lifetime, alternative logging storage) must be timeboxed, documented, and approved by Security + Risk Council.

Exception workflow (summary)

1. Submit exception request in Jira (SEC-EXC). Include justification, compensating controls, impacted assets, duration, and rollback plan.
2. Security performs technical review and assigns residual risk rating (Low/Medium/High).
3. Risk Council approval required for Medium/High; Low may be approved by Security with owner acceptance.
4. Exception granted with explicit expiry date and automated reminders at 30/14/7 days before expiry.

Compensating controls examples

- If extended token lifetime is needed: require IP allowlist for the token, mandatory device-bound auth, and additional audit logging exported to WORM.
- If log retention cannot meet default policy: require snapshotting of critical audit events to the Evidence Repository daily.

Monitoring and revocation

- Exceptions are monitored via Compliance Dashboard; any deviation or new evidence of risk triggers immediate re-evaluation and potential revocation.

Appendices

A. Quick operational checklist for new production service

- Complete threat model and design review.
- Configure RBAC roles and test with least-privilege user.
- Enable structured audit logging and verify ingestion to SIEM.
- Tag data classification and validate retention routing.
- Configure CI/CD gates and SAST tools.
- Register service in asset inventory and evidence catalog.

B. Minimum log JSON schema (example)

{"timestamp":"2026-03-04T12:00:00Z","service":"auth-service","instance_id":"i-0123","principal":"user:alice@redwood.example.com","principal_role":"platform-engineer","action":"role.assign","target_resource":"role:system-admin","outcome":"success","request_id":"req-123","correlation_id":"corr-abc","region":"us-west-2","tenant_id":"tenant-789","raw_payload_hash":"sha256:abcd..."}

C. Contacts and escalation

- Security on-call: security-oncall@redwood.example.com (PagerDuty)
- Eng-SRE on-call: eng-sre-oncall@redwood.example.com
- Incident Commander roster: see Confluence page "oncall-and-incident-response/incident-rotation"
